idiom_name: defer { close() } at the acquisition point; a class owner with deinit when the resource outlives a single scope
implementation_notes: Swift's native scope-exit hook is the defer statement: it runs on every exit path out of the enclosing scope - normal return, thrown error, break/continue, a guard body - in LIFO order, so the acquire/defer-release pair is written where the resource is acquired and the classic owner object is unnecessary for scope-bound lifetimes. Where a resource is owned by an object instead, ARC is the destructor: a class's deinit runs when the last strong reference goes away and the compiler inserts the release at its chosen point (after last use, not necessarily at end of scope), which is deterministic about the reference count but not about the lexical scope, and withExtendedLifetime exists for the cases where that difference matters. Structs and enums cannot define deinit, so value-type owners must release through defer or a with-style helper.
pitfalls: defer has no error channel and silently swallows what it swallows: a failing close inside the defer is invisible unless handled deliberately, so flush/synchronize while an error can still propagate.

ARC release is not scope exit: an owner may be deallocated right after its last use or kept alive by a hidden reference (a captured closure, an escaping callback), so deinit timing must not be load-bearing; structs cannot have deinit at all.
A defer placed before an acquisition that can fail still runs, so the deferred body must tolerate 'nothing acquired' (optional handles, guard-let), otherwise the cleanup crashes on a nil handle.
